chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
title: Manhattan Center ball with Dorsey and Goodman's bands
summary: Crawford recalls Lunceford's band being unable to leave the stand at a ball packed with the top bands.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Now, how did you -- did you find it any different playing for white audiences as opposed to playing for colored audiences?
I mean in terms of the audiences. Were the audiences basically the same. I mean the way they acted.

Well, they were colored, Naturally, they were swingers. Whites were jitterbugging, you know, that kind of thing. I never will forget one night at Manhattan Center. I have (inaudible). We played at a ball. It was just a ball, place packed and jammed with all the biggest bands in New York City -- Tommy Dorsey, Jimmy Dorsey, Benny Goodman, just all of them.

Each band was supposed to go on the stand and play for 15 minutes only, no more, no less. Lunceford's band got on that stand, and if I must say myself (inaudible) bunch with us dancing, jitterbugs like [Shoe Birch] and all that bunch. We got up there, and we couldn't get off. That band was exciting, throwing the trumpets in there and catching them, trombones sliding and then catch it with the left hand. I don't know how they did it. Saxophone bobbing and weaving, singing, choral group. We did everything. I imagine But we were considered (inaudible) in the colored bands, more or less society, [Duke's] (inaudible) mixture). Yes, that was something (inaudible).
So you were -- so we've gotten -- where are we now -- where -- I think we're between -- I think we're between Buffalo and Netherland Avenue.
